edits.fix: Change the footer on all six pages to the standard 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' (for example '/ P0MD3-K1-1').

edits.quote: Find every way to cover each shape with blue blocks. Draw each way in its own copy. [3 copies of the small hexagon, which has 2 coverings; 4 copies of the long hexagon, which has 3]
edits.fix: A K-1 child will judge 'done' by filling every copy and will keep looking for a third and a fourth covering that do not exist. Either print 2 and 3 copies, or add 'Some copies may stay empty.'

edits.quote: Change it into the right picture with as few moves as you can. [a move is shown only by the picture labeled 'one move']
edits.fix: Define the move in words so the adult can read it aloud: 'A move: lift three blocks that make a small hexagon and put them back the other way.' The flip distances on the page are correct (2 and 4).

k-1.summary: A strong K-1 band. The problems are hands-on, at actual size, and all correct: the impossible even-area boards in P1, a fewest-greens pattern of 2, 3, 4 that leads to a guess of 5, every covering of two hexagons, flip distances of 2 and 4, and a game where the first player wins on the strips and the second player wins on the hexagon. Only the footer, the move definition and the extra copies in P4 need fixing.

edits.fix: Change the footer on all nine pages to 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>'.

edits.quote: Which of these boards can be covered with blue blocks only?
edits.fix: Delete it. The next two sentences already give the task (cover the ones you can, X the ones you cannot); add 'only' to 'Cover each board that you can with blue blocks'.

edits.quote: Each board below is a big hexagon with two gray holes, and no block may cover a hole.
edits.fix: The diagram already shows the hexagons and holes. Cut the sentence to 'No block may cover a gray hole.' Answers check out: A and D can be covered (4 ways each), B and C cannot.

edits.quote: Could triangle C in Problem 2 be covered with blue blocks and fewer green triangles than you used? Explain.
edits.fix: A child who used 6 greens correctly answers 'yes', so the answer depends on what each child happened to use. It is also the lower-bound proof that P5 asks for again. Fold it into P5 ('...what is the fewest, and why can no one use fewer?') or move it to the adult notes.

edits.quote: with sides 10 inches long ... a triangle with sides 100 inches long
edits.fix: Children are never told that a small triangle's edge is 1 inch. Say '10 small triangle edges along each side' and '100 small edges along each side'.

grades-2-3.summary: Kernel 1 is developed well. The band moves from possible and impossible boards (including G, which has equal up and down counts and still cannot be covered) to fewest-gap triangles (2, 3, 4, 5), holey hexagons, a 10/100 generalization, chevrons (4, 5, 4, 5 greens, never better than blues) and inventing a board. All answers are correct and the boards are at actual size. The edits are small: the footer, two redundant sentences, the ambiguous P4 follow-up, and the inch wording in P5.

edits.fix: Change the footer on all ten pages to 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>'.

edits.quote: Blank small drawings of boards are for recording.
edits.fix: Delete it. P1, P4, P10 and P11 each already say where to draw.

edits.quote: 4 moves: ____  5 moves: ____  6 moves: ____  7 moves: ____ [one column of 4 copies under each label]
edits.fix: A 6-move round trip passes through 6 coverings but its column has only 4 copies, and the blanks do not say what to write (yes/no?). Use plain rows of copies with no per-number columns, and replace the blanks with 'Write yes or no for each number.' The answers are right: 4 and 6 work, 5 and 7 do not.

edits.quote: If you run out of copies, you can draw more on the back.
edits.fix: Delete it. The answers need at most 10 drawings and the page has 16 copies.

edits.quote: If you run out of copies, you can draw more on the back.
edits.fix: Delete it. There are 20 coverings and the page has 24 copies.

grades-4-5.summary: An excellent treatment of kernel 2. It goes from all 6 coverings of a small board and its flip graph, to flip distances of 8 and 4, even round trips, chains (ribbons), which chain pairs are possible (2 of the 4), how a flip swaps LR/RL, proofs of minimality and parity, and finally counting 20 coverings with one chain and 20 with two. Every diagram and expected answer checks out. There is more work than the hour allows. The edits are minor: the footer, two 'draw on the back' sentences, a redundant rules sentence, and the P4 recording columns.

overall.strongest: Grades 4-5 develop rhombus tilings, flips and ribbons through a carefully sequenced set of correct, concrete problems, from finding all coverings to proving that flip round trips are even and counting tilings with chains.
overall.weakest: No band has a substantive flaw. The weakest point is small: the footers in all three bands lack the required id, plus a few redundant or ambiguous sentences (K-1 P5 has no move defined in words, 2-3 P4 depends on 'than you used').
